partner_context.their_ambition: CalMac runs Scotland's west-coast lifeline ferry network for Transport Scotland — the crossings that connect the mainland to Arran, Bute, Cowal and the isles. With CMAL fleet renewal underway and Scotland targeting net zero by 2045, the ambition is cleaner, more reliable lifeline crossings, starting with the busiest, most commuter-like gateways on the Firth of Clyde.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the zero-emission, foiling upgrade for the shorter, high-frequency Clyde gateway crossings — Ardrossan to Arran, Wemyss Bay to Bute, Gourock to Cowal — served by fast, near-silent, low-wake foiling ferries that add clean capacity on the lifeline runs while heavier vessels keep the long island legs.

hero.eyebrow: Authority proposal · Transport Scotland · CalMac lifeline ferries
hero.title: Navier × CalMac — the Clyde gateways, on foils
hero.subtitle: A zero-emission foiling layer on the busiest Firth of Clyde lifeline crossings: faster, cleaner links to Arran, Bute and Cowal that fit Scotland's fleet-renewal and net-zero mandate.
hero.what_we_do_together: Transport Scotland and CalMac bring the lifeline network, the harbours and the public mandate; Navier brings the foiling-electric fleet, captain training and the certification path. Together we run the Clyde gateway crossings faster, quieter and zero-emission alongside the renewing conventional fleet.

why_now: Scotland targets net zero by 2045 and CMAL/CalMac fleet renewal is live (dual-fuel and hybrid vessels entering service). A zero-emission foiling tier fits that mandate on the shorter, high-frequency Clyde crossings where speed and clean capacity matter most.
multimodal_fit: Navier slots into the existing Clyde gateway crossings — Ardrossan for Arran, Wemyss Bay for Bute (both rail-connected from Glasgow), and Gourock for Cowal — taking the high-frequency lifeline runs while heavier CalMac vessels keep vehicle and long-haul island legs. Passengers step from ScotRail straight onto a foil across the firth.

journeys_unlocked.label: Ardrossan ↔ Brodick
journeys_unlocked.today: Scotland's busiest ferry route to Arran runs on diesel and is weather-sensitive.
journeys_unlocked.with_navier: The busiest Clyde lifeline crossing, with a fast clean passenger tier — near-silent, zero-emission.

journeys_unlocked.label: Wemyss Bay ↔ Rothesay
journeys_unlocked.today: The rail-connected Bute crossing is a diesel ferry from the Glasgow train.
journeys_unlocked.with_navier: A fast, zero-emission passenger link to Bute straight off the ScotRail service.

journeys_unlocked.label: Gourock ↔ Dunoon
journeys_unlocked.today: The short Cowal commuter crossing still means a diesel ferry.
journeys_unlocked.with_navier: A quick, clean Cowal commuter crossing — low-wake and quiet across the firth.

differentiation.why_navier: Proven in service and purpose-built for these crossings: 10x more efficient than a planing hull, low-wake, near-silent and zero-emission. It adds fast, clean passenger capacity on the busiest Clyde lifeline gateways and fits Scotland's fleet-renewal programme.

proof_points.claim: CalMac is Scotland's lifeline ferry network.
proof_points.evidence: 34 vessels serving 50+ ports on the west coast under contract to Transport Scotland; Ardrossan–Brodick is the single busiest route.
New dual-fuel and hybrid vessels (e.g. Glen Sannox, LNG/battery) are entering service on Clyde routes.

proof_points.claim: The platform is proven in service.
proof_points.evidence: 10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out.

objections.concern: Can a foiling ferry serve a lifeline route?
objections.response: On the high-frequency Clyde gateways, Pioneer II adds fast, clean passenger capacity beside the conventional vehicle ferries — not a replacement for the vehicle-carrying lifeline vessels, which keep running.

objections.concern: What about the long island legs and rough water?
objections.response: Phase one is the shorter, more sheltered Clyde gateway crossings; the long Hebridean legs stay on conventional vessels for now (Oban–Craignure and outer isles are a later horizon).

objections.concern: Is this affordable for public lifeline service?
objections.response: Foiling-electric is ~10x more efficient than a diesel planing hull, so fuel — the largest operating cost — falls sharply; the same public budget runs more frequent passenger crossings.

the_ask.navier_brings: The software-defined foiling-electric fleet, captain training, and the maintenance and certification path, aligned to UK MCA requirements.
the_ask.partner_brings: The Clyde gateway harbours, the lifeline mandate, and the CMAL fleet-renewal roadmap.
the_ask.next_step: Pick the first Clyde gateway — most likely Wemyss Bay–Rothesay or Gourock–Dunoon — for a zero-emission foiling passenger pilot.

close.body: CalMac keeps Scotland's islands connected every day, and the fleet is renewing. Navier is how the busiest Clyde gateways get a fast, clean passenger tier now — quiet, zero-emission crossings to Arran, Bute and Cowal that help Scotland toward net zero by 2045.

end_state.headline: A zero-emission foiling layer across the Firth of Clyde lifeline gateways.
end_state.addressable_footprint: The high-frequency Clyde gateway crossings — Ardrossan–Brodick, Wemyss Bay–Rothesay and Gourock–Dunoon — re-platformed onto foiling-electric passenger vessels, with the Argyll and Hebridean long-haul legs a later horizon.

steady_state.total_corridors: The Clyde gateway crossings to Arran, Bute and Cowal (Oban–Craignure and outer isles later)
steady_state.platform_mix: Pioneer II on the gateway crossings
steady_state.the_opportunity: A fast, zero-emission passenger tier on Scotland's busiest lifeline gateways.

end_state.narrative: Steady state is decarbonised Clyde gateways: the busiest lifeline crossings served by fast, near-silent, low-wake foiling ferries beside the renewing conventional fleet.
